stories.title: Concurrent atmospheric phenomena amplify precipitation extremes under anthropogenic climate change
stories.description: Increasing precipitation extremes in the northern hemisphere mid-latitudes affect billions of people. Most destructive events arise when several atmospheric phenomena, such as atmospheric rivers, fronts, cyclones and jets, occur together and interact synergistically. However, how anthropogenic warming alters such concurrent atmospheric phenomena (CAPs), and thereby reshapes regional precipitation extremes, remains unclear. Here we show that CAPs dominate the anthropogenic GHG-driven amplification of extreme precipitation observed over eastern North America and eastern Asia. By 2060–2100, increases in the frequency of CAP-related extremes account for 56–70% of the projected increases in extreme precipitation totals in these two regions and western Europe. Under GHG forcing, strengthened oceanic high-pressure anomalies enhance land–sea pressure gradients and thus increase CAP frequency, while stronger moisture convergence during CAP events raises extreme precipitation probability. Our findings highlight a critical pathway through which anthropogenic warming amplifies precipitation extremes by altering the synergistic behaviour of CAPs. Extreme precipitation events are increasing in many regions. Here the authors discuss how the increasing concurrence of atmospheric phenomena could contribute to these trends under anthropogenic warming.

stories.title: Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier-lake interactions
stories.description: Ice-contact proglacial lakes directly interact with glaciers, promoting glacial lake expansion and enhancing glacier mass loss. However, quantitative assessment of this effect, relative to climate forcing and topography, is lacking. Here, by mapping glacial lakes worldwide in 2000 and 2020 using deep learning and manual refinement, and estimating water volume, we find that ice-contact lakes increased by 3,567 (+35%) in number, 604 ± 22 km2 (+9%) in area and 66 ± 5 km3 (+12%) in volume between 2000 and 2020. We show that lake-terminating glaciers experienced higher mass loss rates (−0.66 ± 0.16 m w.e. yr−1) than land- (−0.40 ± 0.12 m w.e. yr−1) and marine-terminating glaciers (−0.36 ± 0.13 m w.e. yr−1). Ice-contact lakes explain 11 ± 7% of the mass loss of lake-terminating glaciers globally, whereas climate forcing (43 ± 10%) and glacier geometry (46 ± 10%) are more relevant predictors for ice loss. These findings are important to improve projections of future water availability in glaciated mountain regions and downstream consequences under continued warming. The contribution of glacial lakes to glacier mass loss is unclear. This work maps global glacial lakes in 2000 and 2020 to quantify changes in number, volume and area, showing that they explain 11 ± 7% of lake-terminating glacier loss, with climate forcing and glacier geometry the dominant factors.

stories.title: Antireflective bilayer metasurfaces with complete wavefront control
stories.description: Antireflection coatings are widely used in optical systems to increase transmission and suppress unwanted reflections by matching the optical impedance across a uniform interface. Applying the same idea to metasurfaces is fundamentally more challenging because their wavefront control relies on arrays of geometrically distinct meta-atoms, presenting as a spatially varying optical impedance. Here we show that vertical integration can overcome this limitation by allowing bilayer meta-atoms to act simultaneously as phase shifters and impedance-matching stacks. By treating meta-atoms as multilayer thin films, we derive a design rule that links the effective refractive indices of two independently patterned layers and identifies antireflective bilayer libraries with full 0–2π transmission phase coverage. We demonstrate the approach with a free-standing TiO2/TiO2 metalens operating at 1,310 nm, which suppresses reflection below that of bare glass while maintaining diffraction-limited focusing. These results establish bilayer metasurfaces as a platform for jointly engineering optical impedance and wavefront response at the meta-atom level. A bilayer meta-atom structure engineers the antireflective capabilities of the metasurface, without affecting its full 0–2π transmission phase coverage.
